title: Managing sour crop in chickens
subtitle: Identifying and treating a backed-up crop before it becomes impacted.
excerpt: Sour crop is a yeast infection of the crop, the muscular pouch at the base of a chicken's neck where food is stored before digestion. It produces a sour, fermented smell on the breath and a crop that feels full and soft even after an overnight fast. Caught early, it responds well to supportive management at home.
sourceNotes: Gail Damerow, The Chicken Health Handbook (2nd edn., 2015), crop problems chapter. Merck Veterinary Manual, Poultry Crop Disorders (2022). RSPCA, Keeping Chickens Healthy (2021).

glossaryTerms.definition: The muscular pouch at the base of a chicken's neck where food is stored and softened before passing to the proventriculus and gizzard.
A crop blocked with a hard mass of fibrous material, usually long grass or straw, that the bird cannot pass. A different and more serious condition than sour crop.

content.text: fills during the day as the bird eats, feels like a small beanbag in the evening, and empties overnight to a flat or slightly firm state by morning. A sour crop feels full, soft, and possibly squishy in the morning, and the bird's breath has a sour or yeasty smell. This is the key diagnostic check.
Distinguishing sour crop from impacted crop
Sour crop: the crop feels soft and doughy, like a half-full water balloon. The bird's breath smells sour. The bird is lethargic but usually still mobile.
: the crop feels solid and lumpy, not doughy. The bird eats little and loses condition quickly. Impaction needs veterinary attention.
Isolate the affected bird in a crate with water but no food for 12 to 24 hours. This allows the crop to empty and reduces the food supply to the yeast. Keep the bird warm.
After 12 hours, check whether the crop has reduced in size. A significant reduction suggests normal motility is returning. If the crop is unchanged or larger, contact your vet.

When the crop has emptied, reintroduce plain water and then small amounts of bland wet mash (wet pellets or cooked rice) for 24 hours before returning to normal feed. Avoid fruit and fermented scraps for one week.
A teaspoon of live yogurt stirred into feed may help gut bacteria recover; evidence is limited.

Call a vet if: the crop has not reduced after 24 hours of fasting; the bird is unable to stand; the crop feels solid (impaction); you can hear fluid sounds in the crop on gentle pressure; or the bird has a blue or white comb (severe systemic illness).
Remove long grass and straw from the run. Sour crop is often triggered by an accumulation of fibrous material slowing crop emptying.
Feed fermented scraps sparingly and only to birds with healthy crops. Highly acidic fermented feed is not a problem for healthy birds but can tip a predisposed bird into sour crop.
Ensure grit is always available. Adequate grit supports gizzard function and helps food move through the digestive system promptly.

attrs.cue: The sour crop returns after a week
attrs.cause: Underlying thrush (Candida albicans) infection not fully resolved, or the bird has a predisposing factor
attrs.fix: Consult a vet. Persistent sour crop may require antifungal treatment with nystatin. Ask your vet to examine the bird rather than repeating home management indefinitely.
